summary:
Trans identity and consensual same-sex relations are not criminalised in Singapore. Section 377A, which had criminalised sex between men, was repealed by Parliament on 29 November 2022, and an international news agency reported in June 2023 that the LGBT community felt safer in the change's wake. The same parliamentary sitting passed a constitutional amendment reserving to Parliament, rather than the judiciary, the power to define marriage.

Legal gender recognition is available but difficult. The MPSC report of February 2025 finds the process carries prohibitive cost because genital surgery is a precondition. The same report identifies discrimination, abuse and restrictions affecting transgender students, discrimination in employment, and discrimination and harassment in healthcare settings that discourages transgender people from seeking care. The Ministry of Health stated in May 2020 that it expects doctors to respect patients' preferences and circumstances including sexual orientation, with complaints to the Singapore Medical Council as the recourse, and reported that no such complaint had been received from self-declared LGBTQ patients in the preceding three years.

Statutory protection remains partial. The Workplace Fairness Legislation gives Singapore its first statutory anti-discrimination framework, but gender identity and gender expression are not protected grounds, leaving transgender workers exposed. An international LGBTI organisation's overview updated in March 2026 records that LGBTI organisations still cannot register, a structural gap that persists alongside decriminalisation.

Media regulation carries residue of the former regime. A clause of the national broadcast code groups homosexuality with paedophilia and incest as forbidden lifestyles, prompting calls for review in July 2025 from a former radio DJ and actor who argued the grouping has no place in a post-377A Singapore. The media regulator limits the promotion or glamorisation of the homosexual lifestyle on television and radio and imposes higher age ratings of NC16, M18 or R21 on shows or films depicting same-sex sexual activity. In 2019 a rapper withdrew from a TEDx radio talk after being asked not to make sensitive comments about his sexuality.

Public-order provisions still reach sexual and expressive conduct. Section 294 of the Penal Code covers obscene acts in public places with a maximum of three months' imprisonment, a fine, or both. Between 1990 and 1994 gay men were charged with soliciting in 11 cases, with fines of S$200 to S$500. Pride expression continues regardless: Pink Dot SG has been held annually since 2009, drawing record crowds of approximately 28,000 in recent years.

The Singapore Prison Service reported in November 2023 that 10 transgender inmates were behind bars and that no cases of assault against them had been recorded, a rare official datum on trans prisoners. Gender-neutral toilets exist at Yale-NUS College and Tembusu College of the National University of Singapore, and a female toilet was temporarily converted to a gender-neutral one during Wikimania 2023 at the Suntec Singapore Convention and Exhibition Centre in August 2023. That conversion drew public backlash, including a threatened boycott of the venue and petitions against it; Pink Dot SG and the non-profit group Oogachaga responded that gender-neutral toilets complement gendered toilets rather than replace them.

Singapore does not recognise same-sex relationships in any form, whether marriage, civil unions or domestic partnerships, and does not generally recognise adoption of children by same-sex couples. Same-sex couples consequently cannot access the healthcare benefits, inheritance rights or social security benefits available to married heterosexual couples, a constraint that also bears on visitors travelling with a partner.
tangentialFactors:
The Freedom and Marriage Global Barometers country profile for Singapore carries interactive scores across unified, gay and transgender rights indices and an LGBTQI+ perception index covering 2011 to 2024, spanning de jure protections and lived experience; the underlying scores are not reproduced here.

A visitor-facing travel operator describes a thriving LGBTQIA+ social scene in Singapore, citing gay-friendly bars such as Backstage Bar in Chinatown alongside pop-ups and exhibitions, and notes that government representatives stated as far back as 2014 that gay bars and clubs operate in the country. Public attitudes are comparatively open on some measures: a 2021 TODAY Youth Survey found 80% of respondents willing to work with LGBTQ people, 75% willing to form close friendships, and 58% willing to accept LGBTQ family members, with opposition at 6%, 10% and 18% respectively.

A May 2019 National University of Singapore study estimated 210,000 men who have sex with men in Singapore, more than double the previous estimate of 90,000, who could be at risk of a concentrated HIV epidemic. Whether this translates into visitor-accessible prevention or testing services is not sourced here.
localsOnly:
Residents who transition face an employment market without statutory protection on grounds of gender identity, and the February 2025 MPSC report separately records discrimination in employment and harassment in healthcare settings. Students who are transgender encounter discrimination, abuse and restrictions within the education system.

Marriage is closed to same-sex couples. The Women's Charter precedent holds that a marriage not between a woman and a man is void, and the November 2022 constitutional amendment left the definition of marriage to Parliament by simple majority rather than to the courts, keeping a future change legally open but not enacted. In December 2018 a gay Singaporean man won a landmark appeal to adopt his son fathered through surrogacy in the United States; in January 2019 Social and Family Development Minister Desmond Lee said the government does not support the formation of family units with children of homosexual parents through adoption and would seek to strengthen adoption laws, a position that has not been made into law.

A residual piece of state history concerns conversion-therapy-adjacent funding: in January 2006 the Ministry of Community Development, Youth and Sports granted S$100,000 to Liberty League, an ex-gay organisation, and activist pressure led the group to return the grant; it has been defunct since 2014. No general statutory ban on conversion practice is sourced.

Healthcare complaints run through the Singapore Medical Council under the Ministry of Health's stated expectation of evidence-based practice and respect for patients' sexual orientation, a route that in May 2020 had produced no complaints from self-declared LGBTQ patients over three years.

No source in the inventory addresses rules on gender markers in passports or identity cards, visa or arrival screening that could disclose a traveller's trans status, or whether入境 inspection procedures differ for travellers whose documents do not match their presentation. Entry-document questions remain unresolved on this record.

The inventory does not establish whether any hate-crime or aggravated-assault provision names gender identity or gender expression as an aggravating factor, nor whether the Workplace Fairness Legislation's protected grounds will be amended. Its current exclusion of gender identity is sourced; any future amendment is not.

Whether gender-neutral toilet access is available outside educational institutions and convention venues, and whether any national facilities policy exists, is not sourced. The 2023 Suntec conversion and the two university colleges are the only documented instances.
